title: Interstate banking deregulation on credit supply

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects).  
Reason: One group of states lifted interstate‐banking restrictions in period 4 while the comparison group did not.  The treatment therefore varies across units and over time, lending itself naturally to a DID design in which we compare the change in credit supply (log loans/assets) for treated branches before vs. after deregulation with the contemporaneous change for never-treated branches.

Key identifying assumption (Parallel Trends): In the absence of deregulation the average log loans-to-assets ratio of branches located in future-deregulating states would have evolved in parallel with that of branches located in non-deregulating states.  
Additional assumptions: no spill-overs across states (SUTVA) and stable composition of the sample.

## 2. R Code
```r
############################################################
# Difference-in-Differences: Interstate Banking Deregulation
############################################################
# 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------
required <- c("readr", "dplyr", "fixest")
lapply(required, \(p) if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) install.packages(p))
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(fixest)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------
dat <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s05_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Main DID specification: y_it = beta*Treat×Post + α_i + γ_t + ε_it
did_main <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
                  data     = dat,
                  cluster  = ~unit_id)      # cluster at branch level

# 3. Display point estimate & 95 % CI -----------------------
b  <- coef(did_main)["treat_x_post"]
ci <- confint(did_main, "treat_x_post", level = 0.95)
cat("\n=== Main DID Result ===\n")
cat("β (Treat×Post) =", round(b, 4),
    " | 95% CI [", round(ci[1], 4), ",", round(ci[2], 4), "]\n\n")

# 4. Robustness check A: alternative two-way FE with bank-level linear trends
dat <- dat %>% group_by(unit_id) %>%
  mutate(unit_trend = period) %>% ungroup()

did_trend <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period + unit_trend,
                   data = dat, cluster = ~unit_id)

cat("Robustness A – incl. unit-specific trends:\n",
    "β =", round(coef(did_trend)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n\n")

# 5. Robustness check B: pre-trend placebo (periods 1-3 only) ---------------
pre <- filter(dat, period <= 3)
placebo <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
                 data = pre, cluster = ~unit_id)

cat("Robustness B – placebo (pre-treatment data only):\n",
    "β =", round(coef(placebo)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n\n")

# 6. Optional Event-study graph (Sun & Abraham) -------------
# Requires adoption year: 4 for treated, 0 (=never) for controls
dat <- dat %>% mutate(adopt_year = ifelse(treated == 1, 4, 0))
event_mod <- feols(y ~ sunab(adopt_year, period) | unit_id + period,
                   data = dat, cluster = ~unit_id)
# Uncomment the next line to visualise
# etype_plot(event_mod, base = -1)     # need fixest ≥0.11
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition and previous literature (e.g. Jayaratne & Strahan, 1996) imply that deregulation intensifies banking competition, lowers funding costs, and expands lending capacity. Consequently:

• Sign: β > 0.  
• Magnitude: Deregulation should raise the log loans-to-assets ratio by roughly 0.04–0.06 (≈ 4–6 %).  
Robustness A should yield a slightly smaller but still positive coefficient, while the placebo test should produce a statistically insignificant estimate, supporting the parallel-trends assumption.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=deregulated states, control=still-regulated; shock=deregulation date
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Credit supply increases significantly after deregulation
